text: State, transition, base cases, order: tables filled from small to large.
**Recurrence** (递推) builds the answer for size i from answers already found for smaller sizes, filling a table from the bottom up. Write down all four parts before coding.

items.p: What f[i] means, in one sentence.
How f[i] is made from earlier entries.
The first entries, set by hand.
Fill so every entry needed is already known.

title: Climbing stairs: one or two steps at a time
The four parts for the stairs
rows: f[i] = number of ways to reach step i
the last move was 1 step (from i − 1) or 2 steps (from i − 2): f[i] = f[i−1] + f[i−2]

text: The values grow like Fibonacci numbers: f[5000] has over 1000 digits, so the table holds big numbers from chapter 8 (P1255). Only the last two entries are needed, so two variables replace the whole table.
A bee walking from cell m to cell n is the same recurrence with n − m steps (P2437).
A pawn moves only right or down. Ways to reach a cell = ways to the cell **above** + ways to the cell on the **left**. Blocked cells (✕) have 0 ways. Fill row by row, so both neighbours are ready.
In the starting grid, 9 = 5 (above) + 4 (left). The first row and first column have exactly 1 way each until a blocked cell cuts them off.
Shifting every coordinate by 1 gives the table a row 0 and column 0 of zeros, so the edges need no special case. The counts reach about 10¹⁷ on a 20 × 20 board: use `long long` (P1002).
Some transitions add up **many** earlier entries, not just two.
Stack output orders split by where the first element leaves: f[i] = Σ f[k] · f[i−1−k], the Catalan numbers (P1044). "Prepend a number at most half of the current one" sums f[1 … i/2] (P1028).
Count the ways to spend exactly m on distinct dishes. Add dishes one at a time; with dish a, every amount j gains the ways that reached j − a before (P1164).
Loop j **downwards**. Going upwards would let the same dish be used again within one round.
Tiling a 2 × n wall with dominoes and L shapes: list how the right end can look, and write one transition per shape (P1990).
Solve the same problem on smaller input: Hanoi, memoisation, nested text, divide and conquer.

**Recursion** (递归) writes the answer in terms of the same problem on smaller input, top down. It suits nested structure: brackets inside brackets, a board split into quarters, a string built from copies of itself.
To move n disks, trust the function to move n − 1: clear them to the spare peg, move the largest, then bring the n − 1 back. The base case n = 0 does nothing. The count is 2ⁿ − 1.

Write the recursive call as if it already works for smaller n; then only one level has to be right. Moving black and white pieces into alternate order (P1259) has the same "solve n from n − 1" structure.
The plain recursion calls itself several times per level and explodes. Only 20 × 20 × 20 different arguments can occur, so store each result the first time (P1464).
Keep the guard order exactly as the statement gives it: the "≤ 0" rule comes before the "> 20" rule.

A bracket inside the text is the same problem again: the decoder calls itself at "[" and returns at the matching "]" (P1928). An exponent written in powers of 2 is again "write a number in powers of 2" (P1010).

title: Divide and conquer: halves and quarters

text: Each doubling appends a copy rotated by one place. A position in the second half maps back to one position in the first half, so halve until it lies inside the original string: O(log n) steps even for n = 10¹⁸ (P3612).

Board and picture problems split the same way: a 2ᵏ board with one missing cell is covered by one L shape in the centre plus four quarters (P1228); the totem picture is three copies of the smaller picture (P1498).
